items.prompt: In each iteration of force-directed placement, where is each free cell pulled?
choices: Toward the average position of its wire-connected neighbors, plus a weak pull to the center
Toward the farthest corner of the chip to maximize wire box area
Directly onto the nearest fixed pad regardless of its nets
To a random coordinate on every iteration
items.explain: Wires act like rubber bands pulling each free cell toward its neighbor average, combined with a gentle pull toward the center.

items.prompt: What happens if the step size α (alpha) is set too large?
choices: Fixed pads detach and drift toward the center
Cells barely move from their starter positions
Free cells overshoot and pile up together into a collapsed heap
HPWL automatically reaches the exact golden minimum of 14
items.explain: Too much alpha (or too many rounds) stacks cells on top of each other, whereas too little alpha barely moves them.

items.prompt: Because default force-directed placement reduces HPWL from 52 to about 18.7, it acts as a complete legalizer that guarantees the minimum possible wirelength.
items.explain: Force-directed placement is a cheap, continuous move (52 → ≈18.7) that improves wirelength without claiming the compact golden 14 or full legalization.

items.prompt: When reporting results from force-directed placement, what must you ensure?
choices: Compare before and after HPWL using the exact same net model (and verify cells have not collapsed)
Switch from a bounding-box net model to a clique model after running to make HPWL look smaller
Move fixed pads inward along with free cells
Report only the final HPWL number without starter metrics or cell coordinates
items.explain: Using the same net model ('same ruler · same nets') before and after—while keeping fixed pads anchored and checking for cell pile-ups—makes HPWL comparisons valid.
